items.prompt: What is the SI unit of absolute temperature?

options.label: Celsius (°C)
Kelvin (K)
Watt (W)
Joule (J)

rubric: The kelvin is the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature.
Celsius is a common scale but not the SI absolute unit; joules and watts measure energy and power.

items.prompt: The first law of thermodynamics, with W as work done by the system, is written as which equation?

options.label: ΔU = Q − W
ΔU = Q / W
ΔU = Q × W
ΔU = W − Q

rubric: Change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system.
Distractors reverse the sign or use a product or ratio, which do not express energy conservation.

items.prompt: Which statement is the zeroth law of thermodynamics?

options.label: Heat never flows spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body unless external work is done on the system
The entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as its temperature approaches absolute zero
If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, A and B are in equilibrium with each other
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only transferred as heat or work or converted between forms

rubric: The zeroth law states that thermal equilibrium is transitive, which makes temperature well defined.
Other options describe a reversed second law, the first law and the third law.

items.prompt: Which equation is the ideal gas law?

options.label: PV = nR/T
P = nRTV
PT = nRV
PV = nRT

rubric: The ideal gas law is PV = nRT.
Other options rearrange the variables incorrectly.

items.prompt: Which statement is a standard form of the second law of thermodynamics?

options.label: Temperature is the same for all bodies in contact
Pressure times volume is constant for a fixed amount of gas
The entropy of an isolated system never decreases
The internal energy of an isolated system is constant

rubric: The second law says the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease.
The distractors are the first law, a zeroth law idea and Boyle's law.

items.prompt: Which of the following are state functions, meaning they depend only on the current state of a system and not on the path taken? Select all that apply.

options.label: Heat transferred
Work done
Entropy
Pressure
Internal energy

rubric: Internal energy, entropy and pressure are properties of the state.
Heat and work depend on the path, so learners who treat them as properties of the system are mistaken.

items.prompt: A gas in a cylinder with a movable piston is slowly expanded while the cylinder sits in a large water bath that keeps the gas temperature constant throughout. What is the name for this kind of process?

options.label: Isothermal
Isochoric
Isobaric
Adiabatic

rubric: Constant temperature defines an isothermal process.
Adiabatic means no heat exchange, isochoric constant volume and isobaric constant pressure.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes heat from temperature?

options.label: Heat is a quantity of energy stored inside a body and rising with its size; temperature is the energy that flows when two bodies touch
Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference; temperature reflects average molecular kinetic energy
Heat is the average kinetic energy of a body's molecules; temperature is the energy transferred when two bodies touch each other
Heat and temperature are the same quantity measured in different units on different scales, such as joules and degrees

rubric: Heat is energy in transit; temperature relates to average molecular kinetic energy.
Distractors swap or merge the two ideas, or treat heat as stored in the body.

items.prompt: A fixed amount of ideal gas in a rigid sealed tank is heated from 300 K to 600 K. What happens to its pressure?

options.label: It halves
It doubles
It stays the same
It quadruples

rubric: At constant volume, P is proportional to T, so doubling the kelvin temperature doubles P.
Halving inverts the relation; quadrupling confuses it with squaring.

items.prompt: An ice cube melts in a warm room. What happens to the entropy of the water as it goes from solid to liquid?

options.label: It stays constant, since the temperature stays at 0 °C throughout
It becomes zero, since the phase change is complete
It decreases, since the liquid has to release heat to freeze
It increases, since molecules gain freedom of arrangement

rubric: Melting gives more microstates, so entropy rises as heat is absorbed.
Distractors confuse order with energy or assume constant temperature means constant entropy.

items.prompt: A heat engine absorbs 500 J from a hot reservoir and rejects 300 J to a cold reservoir in one cycle. What is its thermal efficiency?
rubric: Work is 500 − 300 = 200 J, and efficiency is 200/500 = 40%.
60% uses the rejected heat as the fraction; 20% and 30% come from other mistaken ratios.

items.prompt: Why can no heat engine operating in a cycle convert all the heat it absorbs into work?

options.label: Gases cannot do work unless their temperature falls to zero
Some heat must be rejected to a colder reservoir by the second law
The first law of thermodynamics says energy input must exceed work output
Friction in the moving parts always removes part of the energy as heat

rubric: The second law (Kelvin-Planck) requires heat rejection to a cold reservoir.
Friction is not the fundamental limit even for ideal engines, and the first law allows full conversion in principle.

items.prompt: An ideal gas expands slowly and isothermally. Which statements correctly describe the process? Select all that apply.

options.label: Its internal energy does not change
Its temperature rises as it does work
Its pressure falls as the volume rises
Heat absorbed equals the work done by the gas
No heat flows into or out of the gas

rubric: Constant T means ΔU = 0, so Q = W, and PV constant means pressure falls.
Saying no heat flows or that temperature rises describes an adiabatic process instead.

items.prompt: A person tries to cool a sealed, insulated room by leaving a running refrigerator with its door open in the middle of it. The refrigerator is powered from outside through a cable. What will most likely happen to the average room temperature over time?

options.label: It will fall steadily, because the refrigerator keeps pumping heat out of the air in the room
It will fall at first and then return to its starting value, because the fridge interior warms up
It will stay constant, because the heat removed inside equals the heat released at the back
It will rise, because electrical work ends up as heat in the room

rubric: Electrical energy enters the room and ends up as heat, so the room warms.
Distractors assume the refrigerator destroys heat or that its removal and release cancel exactly.

items.prompt: An ideal gas expands isothermally while in contact with a hot reservoir. Why must it absorb heat during this expansion?

options.label: Expansion always lowers pressure, so heat must flow in to restore the pressure it lost
Its internal energy depends only on temperature, so the heat absorbed equals the work it does
Work done by a gas always equals its change in internal energy, so heat is needed to match it
Its internal energy rises during expansion, so the absorbed heat supplies that increase in energy

rubric: For an ideal gas U depends only on T, so at constant T, ΔU = 0 and Q = W.
Distractors wrongly assume U rises or that work equals ΔU.

items.prompt: Which of these quantities is a state function of a thermodynamic system?

options.label: Heat absorbed
Heat rejected to surroundings
Work done by the gas
Internal energy

rubric: Internal energy depends only on the state of the system, not the path taken.
Heat and work are path-dependent energy transfers, not properties of the state.

items.prompt: Ice at 0 °C melts into water at 0 °C by absorbing heat. What happens to the entropy of the ice-water system?

options.label: It decreases, because the molecules in the water become more ordered as heat enters
It increases, because the molecules become more disordered as heat enters
It cannot change, because entropy only changes when the temperature of the system changes
It stays constant, because the temperature does not change while the ice is melting

rubric: Melting at constant T has ΔS = Q/T > 0 because the liquid has more microstates.
Distractors assume entropy tracks only temperature change.

items.prompt: Why can no heat engine operating in a cycle convert all of the heat it absorbs into work?

options.label: Friction always wastes some energy, so a perfectly efficient engine is impossible to build
The first law requires the work output to be smaller than the heat input in every cycle
Heat is a lower-quality form of energy, so it is destroyed whenever work is produced
The second law requires some heat to be rejected to a colder reservoir in every cycle

rubric: The Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law forbids full conversion of heat to work in a cycle.
The first law alone permits 100% efficiency; friction is not the fundamental limit.

items.prompt: The Kelvin temperature of an ideal gas is doubled from 300 K to 600 K. What happens to the average translational kinetic energy per molecule?

options.label: It quadruples
It doubles
It increases by a factor of 1.4
It stays the same

rubric: Average translational KE is (3/2)kT, directly proportional to absolute temperature.
The factor 1.4 confuses KE with rms speed; quadrupling confuses it with a squared dependence.

items.prompt: An ideal gas is compressed quickly in a well-insulated cylinder (an adiabatic compression). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: The temperature of the gas rises
The internal energy increases by the work done on the gas
The temperature of the gas must remain constant
No work is done on or by the gas
No heat is exchanged with the surroundings

rubric: Adiabatic means Q = 0, so ΔU equals the work done on the gas, which raises T.
Constant temperature describes isothermal processes, not adiabatic ones.

items.prompt: A student pumps a bicycle tyre quickly and notices the lower end of the pump becomes warm. The pump walls are thin and the strokes take only a few seconds. Which explanation best accounts for the warming?

options.label: Friction in the cylinder heats the air, while the gas itself gains no energy from the compression
The gas temperature rises because its volume shrinks, whatever the energy transfers involved
Heat flows in from the cooler surroundings because the pressure of the gas has risen
Work done compressing the gas raises its internal energy faster than heat can escape

rubric: Rapid compression is nearly adiabatic, so work on the gas becomes internal energy and raises T.
Distractors ignore energy transfer or assume heat flows from cold to hot.

items.prompt: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat from its surroundings and does 200 J of work on a piston. What is the change in its internal energy?
rubric: +700 J comes from adding work instead of subtracting it.

items.prompt: A Carnot engine operates between a hot reservoir at 500 K and a cold reservoir at 300 K. What is its maximum efficiency?
rubric: Efficiency = 1 - Tc/Th = 1 - 300/500 = 40%.
60% and 67% come from using Tc/Th or Th/Tc directly instead of 1 minus the ratio.

items.prompt: A rigid sealed container holds an ideal gas at 1.0 atm and 300 K. It is heated to 600 K. What is the final pressure?

options.label: 4.0 atm
2.0 atm
1.0 atm
0.5 atm

rubric: At constant volume and moles, P/T is constant, so doubling T doubles P.
4.0 atm wrongly squares the ratio; 0.5 atm inverts it.

items.prompt: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 K? Use c = 4200 J/(kg·K).
rubric: Other values come from dropping a factor or misplacing a power of ten.

items.prompt: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 100 kPa, and its volume increases from 0.010 m^3 to 0.030 m^3. How much work does the gas do?
rubric: At constant pressure W = PΔV = 100,000 × 0.020 = 2,000 J.
3,000 J uses the final volume instead of the change in volume.

items.prompt: An engine absorbs 1000 J per cycle from a reservoir at 600 K and rejects heat to a reservoir at 300 K. The Carnot limit is 50%. Which proposed work outputs per cycle are allowed by the second law? Select all that apply.

options.label: 800 J of work per cycle
450 J of work per cycle
600 J of work per cycle
300 J of work per cycle

rubric: Allowed outputs must not exceed 50% of 1000 J = 500 J.
600 J and 800 J exceed the Carnot limit, so they violate the second law.

items.prompt: A heat engine absorbs 1200 J from a hot reservoir during each cycle and rejects 900 J to a cold reservoir. Over one full cycle the engine returns to its initial state. What is the thermal efficiency of the engine?
rubric: Over a cycle ΔU = 0, so W = 1200 - 900 = 300 J and efficiency = 300/1200 = 25%.
75% is the fraction rejected, not the fraction converted to work.

items.prompt: 2.0 mol of an ideal gas at a constant 300 K expands reversibly from 1.0 L to 4.0 L. Using R = 8.314 J/(mol K), how much work does the gas do on its surroundings?

options.label: 6.9 kJ
5.0 kJ
15 kJ
3.5 kJ

rubric: Isothermal work is W = nRT ln(V2/V1) = 4988 J x ln 4, about 6.9 kJ.
3.5 kJ comes from using ln 2 instead of ln 4. 15 kJ comes from using V2 - V1 in place of the logarithm.

items.prompt: A Carnot engine runs between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K and absorbs 2000 J of heat from the hot reservoir each cycle. How much net work does it deliver per cycle?
rubric: 1200 J is the heat rejected to the cold reservoir, not the work.

items.prompt: A gas in a cylinder is compressed so that the surroundings do 150 J of work on it, while 400 J of heat flows out of the gas to the surroundings. What is the change in the gas's internal energy?
rubric: With W as work done on the gas, dU = Q + W = -400 J + 150 J = -250 J.
-550 J and +550 J come from sign errors on the work term.

items.prompt: 0.50 kg of liquid water (c = 4200 J/(kg K), taken as constant) is heated reversibly from 300 K to 350 K. What is the entropy change of the water?
rubric: dS = m c dT/T integrates to m c ln(Tf/Ti) = 2100 x ln(1.167), about 324 J/K.
350 J/K and 300 J/K come from dividing the total heat (105 kJ) by only the initial or only the final temperature.

items.prompt: A monatomic ideal gas (gamma = 5/3) at 300 K is compressed reversibly and adiabatically to half its original volume. What is its final temperature?
rubric: T V^(gamma-1) is constant, so T2 = 300 x 2^(2/3), about 476 K.
600 K assumes T is inversely proportional to V. 424 K uses an exponent of 1/2. 300 K treats the process as isothermal.

items.prompt: For an ideal gas, which of the following processes result in a change in internal energy of exactly zero? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reversible isothermal expansion
One complete cycle that returns the gas to its initial state
Isobaric heating from 300 K to 400 K
Free expansion into a vacuum inside a rigid, insulated container
Reversible adiabatic compression

rubric: Ideal-gas internal energy depends only on T, so isothermal processes, free expansion (Q = W = 0) and any full cycle give dU = 0.
Isobaric heating and adiabatic compression both change temperature, so dU is not zero.

items.prompt: A kitchen refrigerator has a coefficient of performance of 3.0. In one cycle it removes 1500 J of heat from the food compartment. Using energy conservation for the cycle, how much heat does it release into the room per cycle?
rubric: COP = Qc/W gives W = 500 J, so Qh = Qc + W = 2000 J.
500 J is only the work input. 4500 J multiplies the heat removed by the COP.

items.prompt: An inventor claims an engine operating between reservoirs at 400 K and 300 K absorbs 1000 J of heat per cycle and delivers 300 J of net work. Which analysis of the claim is correct?

options.label: It violates the second law, because any engine must reject at least half of the absorbed heat as waste
It violates the second law, because its 30% efficiency exceeds the Carnot limit of 25% for these reservoirs
It violates no law, because 300 J of work is less than the 1000 J of heat absorbed each cycle
It violates the first law, because 300 J of work exceeds the 25% of the input that the reservoirs permit

rubric: Carnot efficiency is 1 - 300/400 = 25%, so 30% is impossible by the second law; energy is still conserved.
Distractors confuse the first law (energy accounting) with the second law, or invent a fixed 50% rejection rule.

items.prompt: An ideal gas expands reversibly from the same initial state to the same final volume, once isothermally and once adiabatically. On a P-V diagram the adiabatic curve falls more steeply. What best explains this?

options.label: The gas cools as it does work with no heat input, so pressure falls from both the larger volume and the lower temperature
In the isothermal case heat leaves the gas, so its internal energy falls faster than in the adiabatic case
The adiabatic pressure is fixed by the heat capacity ratio alone, so it does not depend on the gas's temperature
With no heat input the gas does more work than in the isothermal case, and that extra work removes pressure directly

rubric: In the adiabatic case dU = -W, so T drops and P = nRT/V falls faster than the isothermal 1/V.
The other options misstate the work comparison, ignore temperature, or reverse the direction of heat flow (the isothermal gas absorbs heat).

items.prompt: A student compresses air (gamma = 1.4) reversibly and adiabatically from 300 K to 1/8 of its volume. Step 1: Q = 0. Step 2: use T1 V1 = T2 V2, so T2 = 2400 K. Which step is faulty, and why?

options.label: Step 1: Q = 0 holds only when temperature is constant, so the isothermal law should be used, giving T2 = 300 K
Step 2: the adiabatic invariant is T P^gamma, so T2 follows from the pressure ratio and cannot be found from volume alone
Step 1: compression does work on the gas, so Q cannot be zero and the process is not truly adiabatic
Step 2: T V^(gamma-1) is constant for this process, so T2 = 300 x 8^0.4, about 690 K

rubric: Adiabatic reversible ideal-gas processes obey T V^(gamma-1) = constant, so the student's exponent is wrong.
Distractors misuse the exponent (gamma instead of gamma-1) or confuse adiabatic (Q = 0) with isothermal.

items.prompt: An ideal gas follows a closed cycle on a P-V diagram that is traversed counterclockwise and encloses an area equal to 200 J. Which conclusion follows?

options.label: Net work of 200 J is done on the gas per cycle, which lowers its internal energy by 200 J each time around
Net work over a cycle is zero because the internal energy returns to its start, so the area represents heat only
Net work of 200 J is done by the gas per cycle, so the device is a heat engine absorbing more heat than it rejects
Net work of 200 J is done on the gas per cycle and net heat is expelled, so the device acts as a refrigerator or heat pump

rubric: Counterclockwise traversal means net work is done on the gas; since dU = 0 over a cycle, net heat leaves the gas.
Distractors reverse the direction, confuse dU = 0 with W = 0, or claim internal energy changes over a full cycle.

items.prompt: A Carnot engine operates between 600 K and 300 K. An engineer can either raise the hot reservoir by 50 K or lower the cold reservoir by 50 K. Which option gives the larger efficiency gain, and why?

options.label: Raising the hot reservoir, since efficiency rises to about 58% versus about 54% for lowering the cold one
Lowering the cold reservoir, since efficiency rises to about 58% versus about 54% for raising the hot one
Neither, because real engine efficiency is set by friction and heat leaks, not by reservoir temperatures
Both equally, since each changes the temperature difference by 50 K and so gives the same efficiency

rubric: Lowering Tc gives 1 - 250/600 = 58.3%; raising Th gives 1 - 300/650 = 53.8%.
Efficiency depends on the ratio Tc/Th, not on the difference alone, so the two changes are not equivalent.

items.prompt: An ideal gas expands freely into a vacuum within a rigid, insulated container, doubling its volume. Which statements correctly analyse this process? Select all that apply.

options.label: The gas entropy increases even though Q = 0, because the process is irreversible
The gas temperature is unchanged, because Q = 0 and W = 0 give dU = 0 and ideal-gas U depends only on T
The process can be undone by slowly compressing the gas back, leaving the surroundings unchanged
The gas does work P dV against its initial pressure, so its temperature falls

rubric: No heat flows and no work is done against a vacuum, so U and T stay constant; entropy is a state function that rises because the volume doubles.
Compressing it back requires work and heat rejection, so the surroundings change; the gas does no work against a vacuum.

items.prompt: Two identical blocks with the same constant heat capacity C, one at 400 K and one at 200 K, are placed in contact inside an insulated enclosure and reach 300 K. The hot block's entropy change is C ln(300/400) = -0.288C; the cold block's is C ln(300/200) = +0.405C. Why is the total entropy change positive?

options.label: Entropy is conserved in an isolated system, so the positive total means the calculation contains an arithmetic error
Only the cold block changes entropy because heat flows into it, while the hot block's entropy stays the same at higher temperature
The hot block loses more entropy because it carries more heat, so the total should be negative if the arithmetic is right
The same heat leaves the hot block and enters the cold one, but the cold block's lower temperature gives it a larger entropy gain

rubric: Each unit of heat dQ changes entropy by dQ/T, so the same heat produces a bigger gain at 200 K than loss at 400 K; spontaneous heat flow produces net entropy.
Distractors wrongly claim entropy is conserved, that the hot block loses more, or that the hot block's entropy does not change.

items.prompt: An ideal gas expands freely into an evacuated, rigid, insulated chamber. Its temperature is unchanged, yet its entropy rises. Which analysis explains both facts?

options.label: Q = 0 means the process is reversible, so entropy is unchanged; the rise comes from the lower pressure after expansion
Q = 0 and W = 0, so ΔU = 0, and U depends only on T for an ideal gas; entropy rises because the process is irreversible
Temperature stays constant because the expansion is isothermal and reversible; entropy rises since heat enters the gas
The gas does work on the vacuum that is exactly offset by heat from the walls, so U is constant; entropy rises through that heat flow

rubric: Free expansion has no heat and no work, so U and hence T are fixed for an ideal gas, while S rises as a state function through irreversibility.
Distractors wrongly assume heat exchange or equate Q = 0 with reversibility.

items.prompt: An ideal gas is compressed from volume V to V/2, once isothermally and reversibly and once adiabatically and reversibly, from the same initial state. Which compression needs more work, and why?

options.label: Isothermal, because constant temperature keeps internal energy fixed and the gas resists compression more
Isothermal, because heat must be removed continuously and that extra removal adds to the work required
Adiabatic, because no heat leaves, so temperature and pressure climb higher along the path
Both need equal work, because they reach the same final volume and work depends only on the volume change

rubric: In the adiabatic case the gas heats up so pressure is higher at every volume, and the area under the P-V curve is larger.
Distractors treat work as path-independent or confuse heat removal with extra work.

items.prompt: A heat engine absorbs 1200 J per cycle from a reservoir at 600 K and rejects 800 J per cycle to a reservoir at 300 K. What is the total entropy generated in the reservoirs per cycle?
rubric: The cold reservoir gains 800/300 = 2.67 J/K and the hot one loses 1200/600 = 2.00 J/K, so net generation is 0.67 J/K (the engine's own entropy is unchanged per cycle).
Other options use only one reservoir's change or mismatched temperatures.

items.prompt: An inventor claims an engine takes 500 J from a 400 K reservoir and rejects only 100 J to a 300 K reservoir each cycle, with work output 400 J. What is the flaw in the claim?

options.label: Reservoir entropy would change by -1.25 + 0.33 = -0.92 J/K per cycle, which violates the second law
Heat cannot be rejected at 300 K unless the work output is less than the heat rejected
Efficiency of 80% exceeds 100% of the Carnot value in energy terms, so energy is not conserved
The first law fails, because 500 J in does not equal 400 J of work plus 100 J rejected

rubric: Energy balances (500 = 400 + 100), but total entropy of the reservoirs would fall, violating the second law.
Distractors blame the first law or misstate the limit.

items.prompt: For an ideal gas, why is the molar heat capacity at constant pressure larger than at constant volume, with Cp - Cv = R?

options.label: At constant volume part of the heat leaks to the walls, so less of it raises the temperature of the gas
At constant pressure the gas is reversible, while constant volume heating is irreversible and wastes energy
At constant pressure, heat must supply both the rise in internal energy and the expansion work P dV = R dT per mole
At constant pressure the gas has more accessible molecular degrees of freedom, raising its internal energy per kelvin

rubric: With dU = Cv dT in both cases, the constant-pressure path must also pay for P dV work, giving the extra R.
Distractors invent degrees of freedom changes, heat leakage or reversibility differences.

items.prompt: An ideal gas goes from state (V1, T) to (V2, T) with V2 > V1, once by free expansion into a vacuum in an insulated container and once by reversible isothermal expansion against a piston. Which statements about the two processes are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: ΔU of the gas is zero in both processes
The work done by the gas is the same in both processes
The entropy change of the gas is the same in both processes
The entropy change of the surroundings is the same in both processes
The entropy change of the surroundings differs: zero in one case, negative in the other

rubric: S and U are state functions of the gas, so they match; the surroundings gain no entropy in free expansion but lose Q/T in the reversible case.
Work is path-dependent (zero versus nRT ln(V2/V1)), and total entropy changes differ.

items.prompt: A household refrigerator sits in a small, perfectly sealed and insulated room, with its door open and the compressor running from an outside power cable. A resident expects the room to cool a little. The room's air temperature is monitored over several hours. What does an analysis of energy flow predict?

options.label: The room warms steadily, because the electrical work supplied ends up as heat inside the room with nothing leaving
The room cools steadily, because the evaporator removes heat and the condenser rejects it outside the room
The room stays at constant temperature, since heat extracted inside is exactly returned by the condenser coils
The room cools at first, then stabilises, because the cycle reaches a steady state with equal heat in and out

rubric: The room plus fridge is a system receiving electrical work with no heat leaving, so its energy and temperature rise by the work input.
Distractors count only the heat moved (net zero) and forget the work input.

items.prompt: A Carnot engine runs between 500 K and 300 K. Criterion: largest ideal efficiency gain from a change of 50 K in one reservoir temperature. Which change is best?

options.label: Raise the hot reservoir to 550 K, because it adds more heat input to the engine
Lower the cold reservoir to 250 K, giving 50% efficiency
Both changes give equal gains because each shifts the temperature difference by 50 K
Raise the hot reservoir to 550 K, giving about 45% efficiency

rubric: Base efficiency is 40%; lowering Tc gives 1-250/500 = 50% versus 1-300/550 = 45%.
Distractors assume only the temperature difference matters or confuse heat input with efficiency.

items.prompt: A student argues that water freezing in a freezer violates the second law because the water's entropy decreases. Judge the argument against the requirement that total entropy of system plus surroundings cannot decrease.

options.label: The argument stands, since a spontaneous process in an isolated system may lower entropy at low temperature, as in freezing
The argument stands unless the freezer's electrical work is counted as extra entropy created within the freezing water itself
The argument fails because the released latent heat raises the surroundings' entropy by more than the water's entropy falls
The argument fails because ice has more microstates than liquid water, so the water's entropy actually increases on freezing

rubric: Heat Q rejected to colder surroundings gives Q/T_surr greater than Q/T_water in magnitude, so total entropy rises.
Distractors misstate ice's entropy or apply the isolated-system law to an open subsystem.

items.prompt: Two ideal air-standard engines share the same compression ratio and the same heat input per cycle. Criterion: higher thermal efficiency. Which cycle is better and why?

options.label: They are equal, since the same compression ratio sets the same adiabatic temperature rise in both
Otto, because heat is added at constant volume, so it enters at a higher average temperature than in the Diesel cycle
Diesel, because it avoids the knock limit and therefore converts more of the heat added into work
Diesel, because constant-pressure heat addition takes place at a higher average temperature than in the Otto cycle

rubric: At equal compression ratio, Otto's constant-volume heat addition gives higher efficiency than Diesel's constant-pressure addition.
Distractors confuse the equal-ratio comparison with real-engine advantages like higher feasible ratios.

items.prompt: Heat pump A delivers COP 3.7 heating a house at 295 K from outdoor air at 255 K. Heat pump B delivers COP 5.9 at 295 K from outdoor air at 275 K. Criterion: closeness to the reversible limit COP = Th/(Th - Tc). Which unit is better?

options.label: Neither can be judged, since the outdoor temperatures differ between the two cases
A, because it reaches 50% of its ideal COP of 7.4, while B reaches only 40% of 14.8
They are equal, because both pumps run between the same indoor temperature
B, because its higher COP shows it moves more heat per unit of work

rubric: Second-law efficiency is 3.7/7.4 = 50% for A and 5.9/14.75 = 40% for B.
Distractors rely on raw COP or claim the comparison is impossible.

items.prompt: You must model steam at about 5 MPa just above its saturation temperature. Which statement best judges the ideal gas law PV = nRT for this task?

options.label: It is accurate, since steam is a gas and all gases obey PV = nRT above their boiling point
It is accurate because the high pressure makes molecular collisions elastic, as the model requires
It is poor mainly because steam molecules are polyatomic, and the law applies only to monatomic gases
It is a poor model, since intermolecular attraction and near-condensation behaviour matter at this density

rubric: Near saturation at high pressure, molecular interactions and finite density cause large deviations from ideality.
Distractors treat any gas above boiling as ideal or cite atomicity as the limiting factor.

items.prompt: A company claims a heat engine achieves 45% efficiency operating between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K. Which judgments are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: The claim would be possible if the hot reservoir were 600 K
Better insulation and lower friction could bring a real engine to 45% there
The claim is allowed if the engine is reversible but not a Carnot cycle
The claim would be consistent if the hot reservoir were actually at least about 545 K
The claim violates the Carnot limit of 40% for those temperatures

rubric: The Carnot limit is 1-300/500 = 40%; hot sides at 545 K or above give at least 45% and 600 K gives 50%.
No engine, reversible or not, can beat the Carnot efficiency for its reservoirs; engineering fixes cannot exceed it.

items.prompt: A plant plans to recover waste heat from exhaust at 400 K, with ambient air at 300 K. Vendor X offers a unit with 20% thermal efficiency. Vendor Y offers one with 28% efficiency. Criterion: reject any claim that breaks the second law, then pick the most credible. Which is the best judgment?

options.label: Reject both, since no waste heat at 400 K can be converted to work at ambient 300 K
Choose Y, since higher efficiency is always preferable and engineering can approach unity
Choose Y, because the 25% Carnot limit applies only to reversible units and Y may be irreversible
Choose X, since 20% is under the Carnot limit of 25%, while Y's 28% exceeds it and is impossible

rubric: Carnot limit is 1-300/400 = 25%, so 28% is impossible and 20% (80% of the limit) is credible.
Distractors ignore the bound, invert the reversibility logic, or deny any conversion is possible.

items.prompt: An inventor reports an engine run between reservoirs at 600 K and 300 K. Per cycle it absorbs 1000 J, rejects 400 J and delivers 600 J of work. Which judgment of the claim is correct?

options.label: Possible if the cycle is irreversible, since irreversibility can raise efficiency above Carnot
Possible: the energy balance closes, so the first law is satisfied and nothing more is required
Impossible: 60% efficiency exceeds the Carnot limit of 50% for these reservoirs
Impossible: the first law fails, since the heat rejected must equal the work delivered

rubric: Carnot efficiency is 1 - 300/600 = 50%, so a 60% claim violates the second law.
Distractors confuse first-law bookkeeping with the second-law limit, or think irreversibility can beat Carnot.

items.prompt: A student says that water freezing in a freezer lowers the water's entropy, so the process violates the second law. Which critique is best?

options.label: Water's entropy actually rises on freezing, because the crystal has lower energy and therefore more accessible states
The law applies to total entropy, and the latent heat released raises the surroundings' entropy by more than the water loses
The claim is valid: the second law forbids any local entropy decrease, so a hidden work input must be offsetting it
The law applies only to isolated systems, so it places no constraint on any process occurring inside a freezer

rubric: The second law constrains total entropy; heat rejected to the colder surroundings at lower T raises their entropy more than the water's drop.
Distractors treat the law as applying to subsystems alone, reverse the sign of the entropy change, or dismiss the law for non-isolated systems.

items.prompt: A steam plant must raise efficiency while keeping turbine exit steam quality at or above 0.88 (blade erosion limit). Lowering condenser pressure raises efficiency but drops exit quality to 0.84. Which option best meets both criteria?

options.label: Lower the condenser pressure further, since the efficiency gain outweighs a modest exceedance of the erosion limit
Raise the condenser pressure until quality returns to 0.88, accepting the lost efficiency as the only possible remedy
Raise boiler pressure at fixed inlet temperature, which raises exit quality while also improving efficiency
Lower the condenser pressure and add reheat, which raises exit quality while keeping most of the efficiency gain

rubric: Reheat returns steam to high temperature mid-expansion, so exit steam is drier while the low condenser pressure is retained.
Distractors ignore the stated constraint, give up efficiency needlessly, or misjudge that higher boiler pressure at fixed inlet temperature lowers exit quality.

items.prompt: A text argues: since dS = δQ/T, any adiabatic process has δQ = 0 and therefore dS = 0. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: The argument is correct for all adiabatic processes, because entropy change is defined entirely by heat exchanged
The relation dS = δQ/T holds only along reversible paths, so an irreversible adiabatic process still has dS > 0
The argument fails because adiabatic processes always lower entropy, as no heat can carry entropy out of the system
The relation dS = δQ/T applies only to isothermal processes, so adiabatic ones need a separate and different law

rubric: Clausius's equality uses reversible heat; irreversible adiabatic processes generate entropy internally, so dS > 0.
Distractors treat δQ as the only source of entropy change or misstate the scope of the relation.

items.prompt: One mole of ideal gas expands freely into a vacuum inside an insulated container, doubling its volume. Which method for the gas's entropy change is sound?

options.label: Use ΔS = -R ln 2, because the gas does no work and the process is adiabatic, so the entropy falls
Evaluate along a reversible isothermal path between the same end states, which gives ΔS = R ln 2
Use δQ = 0 for the actual process, so ΔS = 0 because entropy changes only through heat transfer
Use ΔS = Cv ln(T2/T1) with the actual temperatures, which is nonzero because the volume changed

rubric: Entropy is a state function, so a reversible isothermal path between the same states gives R ln 2 > 0.
Distractors apply δQ/T to an irreversible path, mis-use the temperature formula (T is unchanged), or get the sign wrong.

items.prompt: Which statements about Carnot's theorem are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A working fluid with a high enough specific heat can push efficiency to 100% between finite reservoirs
Every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs has the same efficiency, whatever the working substance
The maximum efficiency depends on the reservoir temperatures only through their ratio on an absolute scale
A reversible engine's efficiency rises if its cycle is run with more strokes per second
An irreversible engine between the same two reservoirs has a lower efficiency than a reversible one

rubric: Carnot efficiency is 1 - Tc/Th, independent of the working substance and below that value for irreversible engines.
Distractors claim fluid properties or cycle rate change the limit, which they do not.

items.prompt: Engine A runs between 800 K and 300 K with a measured efficiency of 40%. Engine B runs between 400 K and 300 K with a measured efficiency of 25%. A manager says B is the better design because it is closer to its theoretical limit. Which assessment is best?

options.label: B's 25% equals its Carnot limit, implying reversible, zero-power operation, so that figure is suspect while A's is credible
B is clearly the better design, since it reaches 100% of its Carnot limit while A reaches only about 64% of its own limit, so B wastes less
A's 40% cannot be right, because it exceeds B's 25%, and no practical engine can beat the efficiency of a real engine measured at 25%
Neither can be judged, since efficiency comparisons need identical reservoir temperatures and say nothing about how close each is to its limit

rubric: Carnot limits are 62.5% for A and 25% for B; reaching the limit exactly implies reversible operation at zero power, so B's figure is implausible.
Distractors reward proximity to the limit uncritically or ignore that limits depend on reservoir temperatures.

items.prompt: You must specify a compressor motor for a freezer that removes 2000 W of heat from a space at 250 K into a room at 300 K. Real units reach at most 50% of the Carnot COP. What is the smallest input power rating that meets this?
rubric: Carnot COP = 250/50 = 5, so the real COP is at most 2.5 and the power needed is 2000/2.5 = 800 W.
400 W is the ideal reversible minimum; 600 W assumes a COP above the real limit.

items.prompt: Design a process to double the volume of 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K with zero total entropy generation. Which design meets this?

options.label: Expand the gas adiabatically against a constant external pressure, so that its temperature stays near 300 K
Let the gas expand quasi-statically against a piston in thermal contact with a 300 K reservoir, drawing heat reversibly
Let the gas expand into an evacuated chamber inside an insulated container, so that no heat is exchanged at all
Expand the gas rapidly against a light piston in contact with a 350 K reservoir, to speed up the heat uptake

rubric: Zero entropy generation requires reversibility: quasi-static expansion with heat flow across no finite temperature difference.
Distractors are irreversible (free expansion, finite temperature gap, constant-pressure adiabatic) and generate entropy.

items.prompt: A simple gas-turbine cycle has a fixed pressure ratio and fixed peak temperature. Its turbine exhaust (780 K) is hotter than its compressor discharge air (600 K). Which modification raises thermal efficiency within these constraints?

options.label: Cool the turbine exhaust further before release, which lowers the rejection temperature and raises cycle efficiency
Add reheat between turbine stages, which raises net work and therefore always raises efficiency
Add intercooling between compressor stages, which cuts compressor work and so always raises efficiency
Add a regenerator that preheats compressor discharge air with turbine exhaust before it enters the combustor

rubric: Because exhaust is hotter than compressor discharge, a regenerator cuts fuel heat input without changing net work.
Intercooling and reheat raise work but, without regeneration, raise heat input and can lower efficiency; extra exhaust cooling does not change the cycle.

items.prompt: An inventor proposes a ship engine that absorbs heat from the 288 K sea, converts all of it into work for propulsion, and has no other thermal connections. It is otherwise lossless. What is missing for a valid design?

options.label: A regenerator that recycles the rejected heat back into the working fluid
A better insulated working-fluid chamber so that no energy leaks to the surroundings
A working fluid with a higher specific heat so that more heat is converted per cycle
A cold reservoir below sea temperature to which some heat is rejected each cycle

rubric: The Kelvin-Planck statement requires rejecting heat to a colder reservoir; a single-reservoir cyclic engine is impossible.
Distractors target efficiency details that cannot overcome the need for a second reservoir.

items.prompt: Design an ideal Otto-cycle engine (γ = 1.4) with thermal efficiency of at least 55%, where knock limits the compression ratio to at most 9. Which compression ratio meets both constraints?
rubric: Efficiency is 1 - r^(-0.4): r = 8 gives about 56.5%, meeting both limits.
r = 6 gives about 51% (too low); 10 and 12 exceed the knock limit.

items.prompt: Design a gas model in which internal energy depends on temperature only, with no volume dependence at fixed T. Using (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V - P, which equations of state meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: P = nRT/(V - nb)
P = nRT/V - an²/V²
P = nRT/V
P = nRT/V + bT²

rubric: Any equation of state linear in T with a pure volume-dependent coefficient gives T(∂P/∂T)_V = P, so (∂U/∂V)_T = 0.
The attraction term gives a nonzero an²/V², and the bT² term gives bT², so both break the condition.

items.prompt: A plant has a 900 K heat source and must deliver 5 MW of process heat at 400 K, with ambient at 300 K. The owner also wants electricity, using no fuel beyond what supplies the process heat. Which design best meets this?

options.label: A condensing engine rejecting heat at 300 K for maximum work, with a separate burner supplying the process heat
A heat engine rejecting heat at 300 K, with a heat pump upgrading that heat to 400 K using the engine's own work
Direct heat transfer from the source to the process, throttled down to 400 K, with no engine placed in between
A topping cycle whose engine rejects heat at 400 K, delivering that rejected heat as process heat while producing work

rubric: A topping cogeneration cycle extracts work from the 900-400 K drop and supplies the rejected heat at 400 K as process heat, with no extra fuel.
Distractors need extra fuel, waste the work potential of the temperature drop, or consume the work they produce.
